---
title: "Web interface (architecture)"
---

The web interface (`onthesignal.web`, specification `onthesignal_web.md`) is a user interface
layer: it contains no signal processing (rule R10) and calls the same registry, API, scripts,
reports and assistant as the console.

```text
web.app            onthesignal web: options, security, static files, page, ui.run
web.ui.workbench   one Workbench per browser tab: layout, event polling, palette, shortcuts
web.ui.*           objects panel, tabs (signal, result, editor…), side views, chat, dialogs
web.components     µPlot chart and Monaco editor (Python element + Vue component)
web.state          WebState shared by all tabs: session, terminal, jobs, channels, requests,
                   acquisition, real time, batches, colors of the signals
web.realtime       RealtimeRun: SeedLink monitor and payloads of the real-time dashboard
web.batch          BatchRun: a batch followed file by file, its table and its report
web.terminal       Python terminal: the console running in a thread, VT100 to xterm.js
web.figures        data sent to the charts: decimated, aligned, JSON-safe
web.security       Host/Origin guard, path confinement
plot.spec          FigureSpec: renderer-independent figure and results panel
plot.layouts       one layout per analysis, generic layout, results_view()
processing.display decimation keeping minima and maxima, window statistics
```

## Threads and the event loop

NiceGUI runs on asyncio; widgets may only be touched from its event loop (rule R12). Analyses,
loading, reports, acquisitions and AI requests run as **jobs** (`WebState.jobs.start`), in
daemon threads independent of the browser tabs. Threads never call NiceGUI: they push events
(`open`, `notify`, `form`, `confirm`, `chat`…) into the **channel** of a tab
(`WebState.to_origin` sends to the tab that started the job, `broadcast` to all). Each
`Workbench` drains its channel every 100 ms and follows `session.version`, which every change
of the session increments (`Session.notify`, rule R13).

A thread that needs an answer from the user (assistant confirmation, form of a `/command` typed
in the terminal) calls `WebState.requests.ask(event)`: the tab shows a dialog and calls
`requests.answer`. The wait uses short timeouts so that Ctrl+C still interrupts the terminal.

The worker threads do not inherit the context of the page: `set_session(session,
default=True)` makes the web session the default of the process, so the public API
(`noise(S1)`…) finds it in every thread.

Work that outlives a browser tab belongs to `WebState`, never to a view: the acquisition
(`start_acquisition`, with `acquisition_progress`), the real-time session (`start_realtime`,
`WebState.realtime`) and the batches (`start_batch`, `WebState.batches`). A view or a tab only
reads their state with a `ui.timer`, so a reloaded page shows them again (case W-12). The
job thread of a `RealtimeRun` computes the statistics, the decimated trace and, at a slower
pace, the FFT and the PSD, and publishes them by replacing one `RealtimeView` object (readers
always see a complete payload, with version numbers telling what changed). A `BatchRun` runs
`scripts.batch()` with `on_progress` and `should_stop`. `WebState.seedlink_factory` replaces
the SeedLink client in the tests.

## Python terminal

`web.terminal.PythonTerminal` runs `OnTheSignalConsole` (same namespace, `/` commands and
synchronization as the console) in a thread, with an injected session and display:

- input: the keystrokes of xterm.js go into a prompt_toolkit pipe input;
- output: a `Vt100_Output` and a rich `Console` write into `TerminalWriter`, whose text is
  buffered and written to every attached xterm by the timer of each tab; a scrollback redraws
  the terminal when a tab reconnects;
- `print` of the user code: `sys.stdout` is a `ThreadRoutedStream` that sends the writes of
  the terminal thread to the terminal;
- Enter runs the code when it is complete (`codeop`), otherwise inserts an indented new line;
- Ctrl+C raises `KeyboardInterrupt` in the terminal thread
  (`PyThreadState_SetAsyncExc`);
- `submit(code)` runs code from the editor, the palette or the chat as if typed.

The console offers hooks for the web: `param_form` (graphical form), `ai_handler` (chat),
`edit_handler` (editor), `quit_handler`.

## Figures

An analysis gets an interactive chart through a **layout** in `plot.layouts`:

```python
@layout("my_analysis")
def my_layout(result) -> FigureSpec:
    c = result.curves["spectrum"]
    panel = Panel("spectrum", Axis("Frequency", "Hz", "log"), Axis("Amplitude", "dBFS"),
                  [Series("spectrum", "spectrum")], markers=..., conditions=[...])
    return FigureSpec(result.title, [panel],
                      results=ResultsSpec(headline=["key1"], groups=[("Group", ["k1", "k2"])]))
```

Without a layout, a result gets the generic one (one panel per ordinate quantity, every value
in the results panel), so user scripts are displayed without web code. The chart component is
generic: it draws any `FigureSpec`; colors are palette tokens (`series:0`, `ink2`, `removed`).
`web.figures` decimates every curve (`decimate_xy`, two points per bin, extremes kept) and
aligns the curves of a panel on the union of their abscissas, as µPlot needs one abscissa per
chart.

Adding an analysis therefore takes: the computation and its registration (v2 procedure), a
layout if the generic one is not enough, and its key figures in `ResultsSpec`. The registry
makes it appear in the palette, the *Analyses* view, the forms and the AI tools.

**Heatmaps.** A panel with a `Heatmap` (spectrogram) draws `Result.extra[key]` (`t`, `f`,
`z`) in its plotting area. `Axis.offset` and `Axis.factor` turn the matplotlib dates of the
analysis into seconds from `time_origin` (`(x - offset) * factor`), so that the cursor reads
the UTC time. `web.figures.heatmap_payload` merges the cells into at most 400 × 800 (by their
maximum, so that a narrow line stays visible; on a logarithmic axis the rows are spaced in
`log10 f` and empty rows take the nearest bin) and sends the levels as 16-bit integers in
base64. The browser colors them with the sequential ramp of `plot.style` and reads the level
under the cursor.

**Comparisons.** `plot.layouts.comparison_spec(results, colors)` builds one figure from the
layout of the first result: the curves of result `i` are named `"i/<curve>"` and drawn with
`colors[i]`, the color of its signal (`WebState.color_of`: a signal keeps its slot of the
categorical palette in every view). `comparison_view()` gives the table, one column per
result. `COMPARE_PANELS` chooses the panels compared for an analysis (residual spectrum for
`sinad`); `NOT_COMPARABLE` lists the analyses refused.

**Chart component.** `uplot_chart.js` draws a toolbar above the panels (`buildToolbar`):
full view, previous and next view, *Zoom* and *Move* modes. Every gesture of the user (drag
zoom, move, wheel burst) is a step of the view history: `beginGesture` records the view at
its start, `endGesture` stores it once the gesture is over; Back and Forward apply a view of
the history (`applyView`) and, on a time plot, ask the server for that window. Moving is done
by the component itself (`startPan`, `shifted`), the zoom selection of uPlot being disabled
meanwhile; moves stay within the full view. The component emits `zoom` (time plots reload the
visible window) only for changes made by the user, not for the scale changes that uPlot makes
itself on resize or after building; uPlot runs its scale hooks in a microtask, so the flag of
a gesture is released with a `setTimeout`. `signal_payload(..., margin=1.0)` adds one window
width of data on each side of the visible window (statistics still on the window) so that a
move shows data at once; the envelope always keeps the first and last samples, so that the
full view is the full record. With `live=True` (real-time dashboard), `setPanelData`
re-scales the axes to the new data until the user zooms or moves; *Home* makes them follow
the data again.

## SeedLink with ObsPy 1.5

`seedlink.client.create()` does not use `obspy.clients.seedlink.easyseedlink.create_client`:
ObsPy 1.5 creates the connection of `EasySeedLinkClient` without a timeout, and
`SeedLinkConnection.connect()` then compares the elapsed time with `None`, so that every
connection fails ("'<' not supported between instances of 'float' and 'NoneType'"). The
client is built with a subclass of `SeedLinkConnection` whose `connect()` has a 30 s timeout
(`CONNECT_TIMEOUT`). The timeout is not left on the connection, because `collect()` uses the
same attribute to end the stream when no packet arrives within it, which would cut a
low-rate channel. The fake clients of the tests do not exercise this path: check it against
a real server (for instance `geofon.gfz-potsdam.de:18000`, station `GE.WLF`) after an ObsPy
upgrade.

## Security

`OriginGuard` (ASGI middleware, so it also sees the socket.io WebSocket mounted in the app)
refuses requests whose `Host` is not the server (DNS rebinding) and whose `Origin` is another
site (cross-site requests and WebSocket hijacking); socket.io's own `cors_allowed_origins` is
restricted too. It adds the security headers, with a relaxed content security policy for the
rendered reports only (self-contained Quarto pages). Files are read and written through
`confine()`, which resolves symbolic links before checking the project roots.

## Front-end libraries

µPlot (ESM module registered with `esm=`) and Monaco (AMD build served as static files) are
vendored in `web/static/vendor` with their licenses; see `VENDOR.md` there for the versions
and the parts of Monaco removed. Quasar 2.35, Vue 3.5 and xterm.js 6 come with NiceGUI 4.

## NiceGUI 4

The interface needs NiceGUI 4 (`nicegui>=4.0,<5`), hence Python ≥ 3.11 and, in the browser,
Chrome or Edge ≥ 121 or Safari ≥ 17.2. Points to keep in mind when changing the interface (the
complete list is in the
[release notes of NiceGUI 4.0](https://github.com/zauberzeug/nicegui/releases/tag/v4.0.0)):

- `run.io_bound` raises `asyncio.CancelledError` when it is cancelled, instead of returning
  `None`: let it propagate, and never swallow it in a `ui.timer` callback (catch `Exception`,
  not `BaseException`);
- a cleared text input holds `''`, not `None`: test `not value`;
- element ids in the page are `ng-<id>`: JavaScript code uses `element.html_id`, never a
  hard-coded id;
- a `ui.tab` must be created inside its `ui.tabs`; a table created with `pagination` shows
  pagination controls unless `pagination_controls=False`;
- props keep the names given: `snake_case` names are no longer converted to `kebab-case`;
- lifecycle hooks take functions: `app.on_startup(startup)`, not `startup()`;
- `WEB_CONCURRENCY` above 1 is refused: one server process, which is the model of the
  interface anyway (one server, one session);
- xterm.js 6 paints its viewport itself and defaults to the browser's monospace font: the
  terminal font is set in the options of `ui.xterm`, the viewport background in the CSS of
  `web/ui/workbench.py`;
- Quasar 2.35 wraps the name of an icon in a `<span>`: the browser tests find an icon button
  with `button:has(i:has-text('tune'))`.

## Tests

- `tests/test_web_core.py`: session events, result names, layouts of every analysis, results
  panel, decimation, console hooks — no NiceGUI needed;
- `tests/test_web.py`: security middleware, chart data, heatmaps, comparisons, shared state,
  terminal engine, real time and acquisition with a fake SeedLink client, batches;
- `tests/test_web_e2e.py`: browser tests with Playwright and the Google Chrome of the machine,
  opt-in (`ONTHESIGNAL_E2E=1 pytest tests/test_web_e2e.py`, `pip install -e ".[e2e]"`).
